info.description: One type of ground support equipment, owned by this instance: placed as "belts", the fleet is "belts/AP GSE fleet", and the Turnaround's matching equipment parameter (belt loader, baggage tug, fuel truck, catering truck, GPU, pushback) is pointed at that name. Place one per equipment type. The vehicles start at the home node, the GSE depot; a Turnaround task calls one, it drives empty to the stand over the apron network and is busy there until the task ends, then waits at that stand for its next call. A diesel type counts its fuel burn as power while busy (fuel_kw, 1 l/h = 10 kW of fuel), so the energy summary shows what the fleet burns; nothing is counted while parked. An electric type (Fuel burn 0) carries a battery that its drive kW drains; after a task is released and below a quarter it drives to a charger and works again at 90 %. Place Charger assets (Logistics library) at the GSE depot, sized from the row's charger kW; their grid energy is the fleet's.

info.description: A pool of ramp agents, "AP Ramp crew", owned by this instance: placed as "crew", the pool is "crew/AP Ramp crew", and a Turnaround's "Ramp crew" parameter is pointed at that name. The cabin and hold tasks each take one agent for the task's duration. The shift schedule, when given, sets how many agents are on duty over the day; without one the pool is always at its full size. Place one per crew that works its own stands or rota. Skills are not modelled: every agent can do every task.

info.description: The day's flights. Each row of the model's order book is one flight: its id is the flight id, release is the on-block time, due is the scheduled off-block time, and the free attributes `aircraft` (a type from the AP Aircraft catalogue) and `stand` say what lands and where it parks. The flight leaves by "out" as a FLIGHT entity stamped with entity.flight_id (the order id), so later steps can join their work to one flight. Lateness against the due date is the on-time departure KPI. The book lives in the model (Orders tab, CSV import), not in the asset, so one asset serves any day's schedule. No input port.

info.description: One aircraft stand. A flight arrives by "in", takes the stand (capacity 1: a second flight waits on the apron until pushback) and leaves by "turn_out" for the turnaround; it comes back by "turn_in" when its ground handling is done, frees the stand and leaves by "out". Place one per stand and route flights to it by their `stand` attribute (a DECIDE or ROUTE on entity.stand against the station name). The stand is a STATION and brings its own network node, so put it where the stand really is and draw a taxiway or apron road to it.

info.description: The ground handling of one flight at its stand, between the stand's "turn_out" and "turn_in". Five task branches run in parallel: cabin (deboard, clean, board; ramp crew), hold (a belt loader for the whole branch, a baggage tug and crew to unload, then load), fuel (fuel truck), catering (catering truck) and ground power (a GPU for the whole turn but the pushback). The flight is pushed back once all five of its OWN branches are done: they rejoin on entity.flight_id, so neighbours never swap tasks. A task waits for its vehicle, which drives empty to the stand node, and for its crew. Durations in minutes come from the table, one row per aircraft type (entity.aircraft) and one column per task; the shipped rows put the GPU branch on the critical path so a turn without waiting equals the aircraft's benchmark. Ceiling: the task graph is fixed; a different precedence means editing the asset (upgrade path: a precedence table read by a generic block). Each task branch leaves a task entity (AP_CABIN, AP_HOLD, AP_FUEL, AP_CATERING) that is disposed at the join.

info.description: The meter: whatever the site cannot cover itself is imported and priced on a tariff profile, whatever it cannot use or store is exported up to the export limit, and the rest is curtailed. Import beyond the import limit is recorded as unserved demand rather than silently supplied. Emissions follow a grid intensity profile, so a sustainability assessment is the same run. Place exactly one per site: it is the slack that closes the energy balance. No ports: this is a continuous asset. A demand charge on the peak import power is billed once at the end of the run.

parameters.name: import_profile
parameters.label: Import tariff
parameters.help: Import price by hour of the day, EUR/kWh. A flat tariff is a one-value profile.

parameters.name: export_price
parameters.label: Export price
parameters.help: Paid for every exported kWh: it enters Total Cost as a negative cost.

parameters.name: intensity_profile
parameters.label: Grid carbon intensity
parameters.help: kg CO2e per imported kWh, by hour of the day. It drives Total Impact, which is deliberately generic: use it for water, waste or any other per-unit impact instead.

parameters.name: import_limit_kw
parameters.label: Import limit
parameters.help: Connection capacity. Demand beyond it is recorded as unserved energy, not supplied.

parameters.name: export_limit_kw
parameters.label: Export limit
parameters.help: Largest power the meter may export. Surplus beyond it is curtailed, which the curtailment flow accounts for.

parameters.name: demand_charge_per_kw
parameters.label: Demand charge
parameters.help: Billed once on the highest import power the site actually HELD (the import flow's Peak Rate), the way a network operator bills capacity. 0 for an energy-only tariff.

info.description: Puts the kW a resource, fleet or charger draws on the site bus, so the grid connection prices it. Name the equipment in Source: its busy, idle and other states come from the power it declares, and the draw follows those states through the run. Set Source before running; a name the model does not declare is reported as an unknown resource, fleet or charger. No ports: this is a continuous asset.

info.title: Hub day: electrifying the ground support equipment
info.description: The hub day of the turnaround workload model with its ground support equipment's energy priced and counted: diesel as it is, the same fleets electric at the same counts charging in a night window or whenever a vehicle is free, and the latter with spares. The question it answers: what do energy cost, CO2 and the grid's peak become, do departures stay on time, and does the extra capital pay back? Read on_time_departure, the flow summary (fuel and grid kWh, peak kW), the battery summary (depleted events) and the investment case across scenarios. Illustrative figures.
